costGuide.title: Peugeot EB2FA Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting an EB2FA typically takes 7-10 hours at £65-£85/hr (independent) - confirm exact labour when comparing quotes.
paragraphs: What genuinely moves the price for the EB2FA is the condition of the wet belt system and whether the oil pump has been affected by belt debris - a well-maintained unit with documented belt replacement commands a premium, while an engine with a failed wet belt (and potential oil starvation damage) is a rebuild candidate rather than a simple recon. The EB2FA's three-cylinder design means the cylinder head is prone to carbon buildup if oil changes are neglected. See our full reconditioned engine cost guide

failures.title: Peugeot EB2FA Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Wet belt degradation - oil pump belt failure (the EB2FA's Achilles' heel)
items.whatHappens: Like the Ford 1.0 EcoBoost, the EB2FA (and all PureTech engines) use a wet timing belt system that runs through the engine oil. The belt degrades over time, shedding debris into the oil system and clogging the oil pickup - leading to oil starvation and, in extreme cases, engine seizure. The EB2FA's design is simpler than the turbocharged variants (no turbo-specific oil issues), but the wet belt remains a critical vulnerability. Symptoms include a rough idle, oil pressure warning lights, and eventually catastrophic engine failure.
items.repairVsReplace: Wet belt replacement is a standard maintenance item - budget £600-£1,200 for the job. However, if the belt has failed and oil starvation has occurred, the engine is typically written off. PSA issued a recall for some early PureTech engines for the oil pump belt issue. Preventative replacement at 60,000 miles or 6 years is strongly recommended.

items.title: Carbon buildup on intake valves (direct injection - EB2FA is port-injected)
items.whatHappens: Unlike its turbocharged siblings (EB2DTS, EB2ADTS) which use direct injection, the EB2FA is port-injected (MPI). This means fuel is injected into the intake port, washing the intake valves and reducing carbon buildup - a significant advantage over the turbocharged PureTech variants. Carbon buildup can still occur but is far less severe than on direct-injection engines. If carbon buildup does occur, it typically manifests as hesitation on acceleration or rough idle.
items.repairVsReplace: Carbon cleaning (walnut blasting) is a maintenance item - budget £300-£600. This is not an engine-replacement trigger unless carbon buildup has caused valve damage, which is rare on a port-injected engine.

items.title: Coil pack failure
items.whatHappens: The EB2FA's coil packs are a known weak point. Symptoms include a misfire, hesitation under acceleration, rough idle, and an engine management light. The three-cylinder design means any coil failure is immediately noticeable.
items.repairVsReplace: Coil pack replacement is a straightforward job - budget £150-£300. This is a maintenance item and rarely an engine-replacement trigger.

items.title: Timing chain (EB2FA uses a wet belt, not a chain)
items.whatHappens: The EB2FA uses a wet timing belt, not a timing chain. This is a critical distinction from many other small petrol engines. The belt is oil-immersed and degrades over time, as described above. Unlike a chain, the belt has a finite service life and MUST be replaced preventatively.
items.repairVsReplace: Preventative belt replacement is mandatory - not optional. If the belt fails, the engine is typically written off.

failures.goodYearsLine: The EB2FA is the most reliable variant of the PureTech family - it lacks a turbocharger (simpler cooling and oil systems) and uses port injection (no carbon buildup issues). With strict oil change intervals using the correct 0W-30 spec oil (specifically PSA B71 2312 or B71 2297), and preventative wet belt replacement at 60,000 miles, EB2FA engines can exceed 150,000 miles without major failure. Early EB2FA units (2012-2015) are more prone to belt degradation than post-2016 units.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the EB2FA
variants.intro: The EB2FA is a specific engine code within the PSA PureTech family. It is the 1.2-litre naturally aspirated (VTi) variant, distinguished from the turbocharged EB2DTS and EB2ADTS engines. Confirming your exact code is essential before ordering a replacement. Where to find your engine code: - On the engine: Stamped on a flat machined surface on the cylinder block, typically near the transmission bell housing - On the V5C registration document: Listed under vehicle details - Via VIN: Use an online decoder with your 17-character VIN Commonly confused codes - check you have the right one: - EB2DTS - 1.2-litre PureTech turbocharged (110 hp). Fitted to higher-spec 208, 308, C3, C4 models. The EB2DTS uses direct injection and has a turbocharger - significantly different from the naturally aspirated EB2FA. NOT interchangeable. - EB2ADTS - 1.2-litre PureTech turbocharged (130 hp). Fitted to newer 208, 308, 2008, C3, C4. Higher-output version with direct injection. NOT interchangeable. - EB2DT - 1.2-litre PureTech turbocharged (110 hp, earlier variant). Similar to EB2DTS but with different emissions calibration. NOT interchangeable. - EB2 - Base 1.2-litre PureTech code (sometimes used interchangeably with EB2FA but the 'FA' designates the specific naturally aspirated tune). Always confirm the full code. Why getting the right code matters: The EB2FA is port-injected and naturally aspirated - the EB2DTS/ADTS are direct-injected and turbocharged. They have fundamentally different fuel systems, cylinder heads, pistons, and ECU calibrations. Fitting a turbocharged variant into an EB2FA car is not a straight swap - it requires different wiring looms, fuel system components, intercooler, and ECU. Always confirm your code before purchasing.

relatives.description: - the older 1.4-litre and 1.6-litre petrol engines that preceded the PureTech family. Unlike the EB2FA, the TU-series engines used a traditional timing belt (not a wet belt) and were iron-block designs. The EB2FA's all-aluminium construction and wet belt system were significant improvements for efficiency and weight, but introduced the wet belt degradation issue that older engines didn't suffer.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement EB2FA - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used EB2FA can be a sensible option for lower-value host vehicles (sub-£3,000 208 or C3) - but only with documented service history and **proof that the wet belt has been replaced**. The EB2FA's critical vulnerability is the oil-immersed timing belt; a used unit without belt replacement history is a significant risk. Request evidence of oil pressure tests and oil filter inspection for debris before committing to any used purchase. See used engine guide
options.href: /LINK PENDING - page not in current inventory

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** For most EB2FA owners, a reconditioned unit from a reputable supplier is the recommended choice. A proper recon addresses the wet belt, tensioner, oil pump, and includes a full gasket set. Crucially, a reputable recon will replace the oil pump (or thoroughly clean it) to prevent residual debris from contaminating the new belt. With a 12-24 month warranty, this is the low-risk option for vehicles worth £3,000+. See reconditioned engine guide
options.href: /LINK PENDING - page not in current inventory

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full rebuild of the EB2FA is only justified for high-value examples (low-mileage 208 GT Line, well-specced C4) where the vehicle's value comfortably exceeds the rebuild cost. A quality rebuild should include a new wet belt, tensioner, oil pump, gaskets, and full cylinder head assessment. Given the wet belt vulnerability, confirm that the rebuilder is using genuine PSA-spec belts and the correct oil grade. See rebuilt engine guide
options.href: /LINK PENDING - page not in current inventory

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: ** All replacement options can be supplied and fitted through our network of vetted UK PSA petrol specialists - with warranties that follow the engine, not just the car. See supply & fit
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: ** The EB2FA typically sits in vehicles worth £2,000-£8,000 (208, C3, C4, DS3). A reconditioned EB2FA at £1,100-£1,800 represents 14-90% of vehicle value - **a critical financial consideration**. For sub-£2,500 examples, a used engine from £500-£900 is the only financially sensible route, but only with thorough belt history inspection. For vehicles worth £4,000+, a reconditioned unit is generally viable and offers peace of mind with warranty. Always evaluate the rest of the vehicle before committing - a £1,500 engine in a £2,000 car with a failing clutch and worn suspension is rarely the right decision.

items.question: What are the most common problems with the EB2FA engine?
items.answer: The EB2FA's most documented issues are: (1) wet belt degradation - the oil-immersed timing belt sheds debris into the oil system, clogging the oil pickup and causing oil starvation; (2) coil pack failure - causes misfire and rough idle; (3) carbon buildup - though less severe than on direct-injection variants, carbon can still accumulate on intake valves. Wet belt failure is the most serious - it can write off the engine. Preventative belt replacement at 60,000 miles or 6 years is strongly recommended. Use only the correct 0W-30 spec oil (PSA B71 2312 or B71 2297).

items.question: Which Peugeot, Citroën and DS models use the EB2FA engine?
items.answer: The EB2FA was fitted to: Peugeot - 208 (A9), 308 (T9), 2008 (A94). Citroën - C3 (A7), C4 (B7), C4 Picasso (B78), DS3 (A55). The engine was produced from 2012 to 2018 with 82 hp output. The EB2FA is the naturally aspirated (VTi) entry-level PureTech. Check the engine code stamp on the cylinder block near the transmission bell housing. The turbocharged EB2DTS/ADTS replaced the EB2FA from 2018 onward.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned EB2FA engine?
items.answer: For the EB2FA, reconditioned is generally the smarter choice because the engine's key failure - wet belt degradation - is often invisible on a used unit without stripping the timing cover. However, for lower-value vehicles (sub-£2,500), a used engine from £500-£900 with documented belt replacement history can be viable. Used units risk hidden belt debris in the oil system and oil starvation damage. Reconditioned units include new wet belt, tensioner, oil pump cleaning, and a warranty. Rebuilt is only justified for high-value examples where the car's value exceeds the rebuild cost.

items.question: How do I know if my car has the EB2FA engine and not another variant?
items.answer: The EB2FA engine code is stamped on the cylinder block - look for a flat machined surface near the transmission bell housing, typically on the front or side of the block. The code also appears on the V5C registration document and can be confirmed via the vehicle's VIN using an online decoder. The EB2FA is a 1.2-litre (1,199 cc) naturally aspirated petrol engine with MPI (multi-port injection). It is often confused with the EB2DTS/ADTS (turbocharged variants) - physically different in fuel system, cylinder head, and turbocharger. Fitting a different code requires different wiring looms, fuel system components, intercooler, and ECU.

items.question: How long does an EB2FA engine last?
items.answer: With proper maintenance, the EB2FA can exceed 150,000 miles (≈240,000 km) - but this is dependent on strict oil change intervals and preventative wet belt replacement. The engine's longevity is highly dependent on using the correct 0W-30 spec oil (PSA B71 2312 or B71 2297) and replacing the wet belt at 60,000 miles or 6 years. Use only the correct oil specification - incorrect oil accelerates belt degradation. The wet belt should be inspected regularly and replaced preventatively. Early EB2FA units (2012-2015) are more prone to belt degradation than post-2016 units.
